repo.description: ### Summary Immich's plugin/workflow system lets a plugin manifest declare `allowedHosts` - a list of hostname patterns restricting where its `httpRequest` capability can reach, intended as a sandboxing boundary. The check enforcing this is broken: it builds a regex from each pattern but never anchors it, so the match succeeds if the allowed hostname appears anywhere as a substring of the target, not just as an exact match. Any attacker-controlled domain that embeds the allowed hostname (e.g. `trusted-partner.example.com.attacker-controlled.net`) bypasses the restriction completely. ### Details In `server/src/services/workflow-execution.service.ts`, the `httpRequest` host function checks each `allowedHosts` pattern like this: ```ts const regex = new RegExp(pattern.replaceAll('.', String.raw`\.`).replaceAll('*', '.*')); if (regex.test(hostname)) { // request permitted } ``` There are no `^`/`$` anchors. A pattern like `trusted-partner.example.com`, meant to restrict requests to that exact host, will also match `trusted-partner.example.com.attacker-controlled.net`, `nottrusted-partner.example.com`, or any string containing that substring. This defeats the entire purpose of `allowedHosts` as a security boundary - a plugin manifest can display a narrow, trustworthy-looking restriction while actually being able to reach arbitrary attacker-controlled infrastructure. ### PoC Reproduced in three layers, from isolated logic to full live GUI exploitation: **1. Isolated logic verification** (real Node.js, exact vulnerable code): **2. In-container live network test**: ran the identical check inside the running `immich_server` container against a real internal-only listener reachable via a lookalike domain. Result: `allowed: true`, followed by a successful `fetch()` (`status: 200`) reaching the internal target. **3. Full end-to-end GUI exploitation (primary evidence)**: Built and installed a real, compiled WASM plugin (`test-ssrf-plugin`) declaring method `restrictedPing` with `"allowedHosts": ["trusted-partner.example.com"]`. Created a workflow via Immich's Workflows UI (Trigger: `AssetCreate`; Step: `Restricted Ping`, `url: http://trusted-partner.example.com.attacker-controlled.net:8000/`). Uploaded a test photo through the ordinary Immich UI - no terminal access involved in the trigger itself. This fired the workflow, which called `httpRequest()`, which the broken check incorrectly approved. The internal listener's access log confirmed the request arrived: The `POST` method matches the plugin's code (`functions.httpRequest(config.url, { method: 'POST' })`) exactly, confirming this was real workflow execution triggered by normal product usage. ### Impact Any plugin declaring `allowedHosts` for sandboxing provides no real security boundary - the restriction is trivially bypassable by anyone who can register a domain containing the allowed hostname as a substring. This undermines the trust model an admin relies on when reviewing/installing a plugin claiming restricted network access. A malicious or compromised plugin can reach attacker-controlled infrastructure, internal-only services, or cloud metadata endpoints while displaying an innocuous, narrowly-scoped `allowedHosts` declaration. **Suggested remediation:** Anchor the regex and use safer wildcard semantics: ```ts const escaped = pattern.replaceAll('.', '\\.').replaceAll('*', '[^.]*'); const regex = new RegExp(`^${escaped}$`); ``` Using `[^.]*` instead of `.*` for `*` also ensures a wildcard matches only a single hostname label, consistent with standard hostname-wildcard conventions.
repo.summary: Unanchored Regex Allows Complete Bypass of Plugin allowedHosts SSRF Protection
